Several features are associated with aesthetic experiences, but it is controversial whether any of them are essential. Aesthetic experiences usually appreciate an object for its own sake because of its sensory properties, resulting in aesthetic pleasure from a positive evaluation of the object. This pleasure is typically said to be detached from practical concerns and can involve selfless absorption, allowing imaginative freedom or free play of [[Mind|mental faculties]] in addition to sensory perception. Some theorists associate this free play with an absence of conceptual activity. Aesthetic experiences may also be [[Normativity|normative]], meaning that certain responses are appropriate, like the positive appreciation of beauty, but others are not, such as the positive appreciation of ugliness.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Peacocke|2024|loc=§ 2. Mental Aspects of Aesthetic Experience}} | {{harvnb|Stecker|2010|pp=40–41, 47, 53–54, 58–59}} }}</ref>

A central aspect of aesthetic experience is the aesthetic attitude{{em dash}}a special way of observing or engaging with art and nature. This attitude involves a form of pure appreciation of perceptual qualities detached from personal [[desire]]s and practical concerns. It is disinterested in this sense by engaging with an object for its own sake without ulterior motives or practical consequences.{{efn|For instance, [[Roger Scruton]] argues that the aesthetic attitude has three basic elements: it is done for its own sake, it aims at pleasure, and it involves a normative judgment, implying an intersubjective agreement about the assessed aesthetic value.<ref>{{harvnb|King|loc=§ 3c. Scruton}}</ref>}} For example, the experience of a violent storm through the aesthetic attitude may focus on its intricate patterns of lightning and thunder rather than preparing for its immediate dangers. One characterization understands the aesthetic attitude as a natural form of apprehension that occurs on its own in certain situations. Another outlook holds that the aesthetic attitude is a [[Voluntary action|voluntary]] stance people can choose to adopt toward any object.<ref name="Bunnin 2004 15">{{multiref | {{harvnb|Bunnin|Yu|2004|p=15}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=4–6}} | {{harvnb|Shelley|2022|loc=§ 2.3 The Aesthetic Attitude}} }}</ref> There is debate about the extent and type of emotional engagement a disinterested stance requires, for instance, whether fear during a [[horror movie]] can be disinterested.<ref>{{harvnb|Shelley|2022|loc=§ 2.3 The Aesthetic Attitude}}</ref>{{efn|A similar problem is addressed by the [[paradox of fiction]]: the challenge of explaining how fictional scenarios evoke real emotional responses and whether these responses are rational.<ref>{{harvnb|Schneider|loc=Lead section}}</ref>}}

The aesthetic attitude is sometimes contrasted with other attitudes, such as the practical attitude, which is interested in usefulness and seeks to utilize or manipulate objects to achieve specific goals. Similarly, it differs from the scientific attitude, which aims to explain phenomena and acquire [[Declarative knowledge|factual knowledge]] about the world.<ref name="Bunnin 2004 15"/> Some philosophers, such as [[Arthur Schopenhauer]] and [[Martin Heidegger]], suggest that the aesthetic attitude can reveal aspects of reality obscured in other attitudes.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Shelley|2022|loc=§ 2.3 The Aesthetic Attitude}} | {{harvnb|Peacocke|2024|loc=§ 1.5 Fundamental Nature}} | {{harvnb|Bunnin|Yu|2004|p=15}} }}</ref>

Aesthetic experience is further associated with aesthetic pleasure{{em dash}}a form of enjoyment in response to natural and artistic beauty. It is typically characterized as disinterested pleasure. It contrasts with interested pleasure that arises from the satisfaction of desires, such as the joy of achieving a personal goal or indulging in a particular type of [[Food craving|food one craves]]. Another difference is that aesthetic pleasure does not depend on the existence of the enjoyed object, like enjoying the beauty of a sunset in a [[dream]]. The joy in achieving a personal goal, by contrast, would be frustrated if one discovered that the achievement was merely a dream.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Bunnin|Yu|2004|p=16}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=13–14}} }}</ref> Philosophers like [[Immanuel Kant]] argue that aesthetic pleasure is preconceptual, meaning that it arises from a free interplay between imagination and understanding rather than from cognitive judgments or conceptual analysis.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Bunnin|Yu|2004|p=16}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|p=5}} | {{harvnb|Ginsborg|2022|loc=§ 2.2 How Are Judgments of Beauty Possible?, § 2.3.2 The Free Play of Imagination and Understanding}} }}</ref> One view distinguishes refined from unrefined aesthetic pleasures based on whether the pleasure is evoked by a cultivated taste or an immediate, instinctual response.<ref name="Townsend 2006 13–14">{{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=13–14}}</ref>

Aesthetic pleasure is central to the characterization of many aesthetic phenomena that are said to involve or evoke such pleasure. However, the view that aesthetic pleasure is the defining characteristic of the entire aesthetic domain is controversial. It faces challenges in explaining phenomena such as the sublime, [[drama]], [[tragedy]], and forms of [[modern art]], which may evoke diverse emotions not primarily linked to pleasure.<ref name="Townsend 2006 13–14"/>

=== Aesthetic judgments and taste ===
<!--'Aesthetic judgement' and 'Aesthetic judgment' redirect here-->
[[File:Immanuel Kant - Gemaelde 1.jpg|thumb|upright=.8|left|alt=Oil painting of Immanuel Kant|In his 1790 book ''[[Critique of Judgment]]'', [[Immanuel Kant]] argued that aesthetic judgments are subjective, universal, disinterested, and involve an interplay of sense, imagination, and understanding.<ref name="auto10">{{multiref | {{harvnb|Stecker|2010|pp=40–41}} | {{harvnb|Ginsborg|2022|loc=Lead section, § 2.2 How Are Judgments of Beauty Possible?, § 2.3.2 The Free Play of Imagination and Understanding}} }}</ref>]]

Aesthetic judgments are assessments of the aesthetic features and values of objects, expressed in statements like "this music is beautiful". They can apply both to natural objects and artworks. Aesthetic judgments also include assessments about how or why an object has aesthetic value without explicitly determining its overall aesthetic worth, as in the statement "this music is balanced". Many debates in aesthetics concern the nature of aesthetic judgments, in particular, whether they can be as objective and universal as [[empirical]] judgments made by [[Natural science|natural scientists]]. Subjectivists argue that aesthetic judgments express personal feelings and dislikes without universal validity. This view is contested by objectivists, who hold that aesthetic judgments describe objective features that are independent of the particular [[preference]]s of the judging individual. Intermediate views suggest that the standards of aesthetic judgment are grounded in stable shared dispositions rather than variable individual preferences, resulting in a form of subjective universality.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Bunnin|Yu|2004|p=16}} | {{harvnb|Zangwill|1998|pp=78–79, 85–86, 90}} }}</ref> This position is reflected in Kant's view, which identifies four core features of aesthetic judgments: they are subjective, universal, disinterested, and involve an interplay of sense, imagination, and understanding.<ref name="auto10"/>

Philosophers such as [[Francis Hutcheson (philosopher)|Francis Hutcheson]] and [[David Hume]] argue that there are general aesthetic principles or universal criteria that are applied when making aesthetic judgments. Particularists, by contrast, assert that the unique nature of each aesthetic object requires a case-by-case evaluation that cannot be fully subsumed under general principles.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Shelley|2022|loc=§ 2.2 Aesthetic Judgment}} | {{harvnb|Bender|1995|p=379}} }}</ref> A related debate between rationalism and the immediacy thesis concerns whether aesthetic judgments are mediated through concept application and [[reasoning]] or emerge directly from sensory [[intuition]].<ref>{{harvnb|Shelley|2022|loc=§ 1. The Concept of Taste}}</ref>

Aesthetic judgments rely on taste,{{efn|In biology, the term ''taste'' has a narrower meaning limited to the [[gustatory system]].<ref>{{harvnb|Korsmeyer|2013|p=258}}</ref>}} which is a sensitivity to aesthetic qualities, a capacity to feel aesthetic pleasure, or an ability to discern beauty and other aesthetic qualities. Taste is a type of preference expressed in immediate reactions and is sometimes understood as an inner sense or cognitive faculty. Differences in taste are often used to explain why people disagree about aesthetic judgments and why the judgments of some people, such as art critics with extensive experience and a refined sense, carry more weight than those of casual observers. Taste varies both among cultures and among individuals within a culture.{{efn|Taste is also influenced by a person's upbringing.<ref>{{harvnb|Bunnin|Yu|2004|p=678}}</ref> For example, the sociologist [[Pierre Bourdieu]] argued that taste is mostly determined by [[social class]] and cultural context, leading to significant differences in [[working class]] and [[upper class]] tastes.<ref>{{harvnb|Spicher ''Aesthetic Taste''|loc=§ 5a. Pierre Bourdieu}}</ref>}} There are also some cross-cultural agreements. Several philosophers argue that taste can be learned to some extent and that the judgments of experienced observers follow similar standards, suggesting the existence of social norms of right and wrong aesthetic assessments.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Bunnin|Yu|2004|p=678}} | {{harvnb|Tregenza|2005}} | {{harvnb|Shelley|2022|loc=§ 1. The Concept of Taste}} | {{harvnb|Cohen|2004|pp=167–170}} | {{harvnb|Korsmeyer|2013|pp=257–258}} }}</ref>

The term "aesthetic universal" refers to aspects of taste and other aesthetic phenomena that are shared across different cultures and societies, indicating common features of human nature underlying aesthetics. Suggested general tendencies include the dispositions to engage in artistic expressions or to derive aesthetic pleasure from appreciating these expressions. The existence of more specific shared tendencies is debated. An example is the idea that humans generally find [[Savanna|savanna-like landscapes]] with open grassy plains and scattered trees pleasing.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Dutton|2013|pp=267–268}} | {{harvnb|Sheridan|Gardner|2012|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=lRAKnDuBPF4C&pg=PA292 292]}} | {{harvnb|Shockley|2022|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=DgRuEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA44 44–46]}} }}</ref>

== Art ==
{{main|Art}}
Art is a central topic of aesthetics and the main subject of the philosophy of art. It encompasses diverse forms, including [[painting]], [[sculpture]], [[music]], [[dance]], [[literature]], and [[theater]]. This field covers both artworks and the skills or activities involved in their creation. Artworks are artifacts or [[performance]]s typically created by humans. They differ in this respect from naturally occurring aesthetic objects, like landscapes and sunsets.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Bunnin|Yu|2004|pp=52–53}} | {{harvnb|Adajian|2024|loc=§ 1. Constraints on Definitions of Art}} | {{harvnb|Davies|2013a|p=225}} | {{harvnb|Beauchamp|2005|p=15}} | {{harvnb|Levinson|2005|pp=3–4}} }}</ref>

=== Definitions ===
A central debate in the philosophy of art concerns the definition of art or how to [[Classificatory disputes about art|distinguish it from non-art]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Stecker|2010|p=8}} | {{harvnb|Bunnin|Yu|2004|pp=52–53}} | {{harvnb|Adajian|2024|loc=§ 2. Definitions From the History of Philosophy}} }}</ref> There are many theories, each offering a unique perspective on the nature of art.<ref name="auto13">{{multiref | {{harvnb|Stecker|2010|pp=10–11, 120–121}} | {{harvnb|Davies|2013|pp=213–215}} }}</ref>

[[File:Marcel Duchamp, 1917, Fountain, photograph by Alfred Stieglitz.jpg|thumb|upright=.8|alt=Black-and-white photo of a porcelain urinal signed "R. Mutt"|Conventionalist definitions of art assert that art is a [[Social construct|socially constructed]] category. They explain that readymade objects like [[Marcel Duchamp]]'s ''[[Fountain (Duchamp)|Fountain]]'' are considered art by reference to established conventions.<ref>{{harvnb|Adajian|2024|loc=Lead section, § 4. Contemporary Definitions}}</ref>]]

Essentialist approaches argue that there is an [[essence]] or a set of inherent features shared by all artworks and only by them.<ref name="auto13"/> They often define artworks in terms of other aesthetic concepts, such as ''representation'', ''beauty'', or ''aesthetic experience''. An early object-centered approach, first proposed by [[Plato]], characterizes artworks as representations that seek to reflect or [[Mimesis|imitate]] certain aspects of reality.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Bunnin|Yu|2004|pp=52–53}} | {{harvnb|Adajian|2024|loc=§ 2. Definitions From the History of Philosophy}} | {{harvnb|Levinson|2005|p=5}} }}</ref> Another definition suggests that artworks are objects designed to evoke aesthetic experiences or pleasure. A related approach proposes that all artworks have certain aesthetic properties in common, such as beauty.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Stecker|2010|p=8}} | {{harvnb|Levinson|2005|pp=3–4}} | {{harvnb|Davies|2013|pp=213–216}} | {{harvnb|Adajian|2024|loc=§ 4. Contemporary Definitions}} | {{harvnb|Levinson|2005|pp=5–6}} }}</ref> [[Aesthetic formalism]] argues that specific formal features, such as a "[[significant form]]", are the hallmark of art.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Bunnin|Yu|2004|pp=52–53, 640–641}} | {{harvnb|Adajian|2024|loc=§ 2. Definitions From the History of Philosophy}} }}</ref> Artist-centered approaches see artistic activity as the essential aspect of artworks. One conception understands artworks as special vehicles through which artists express emotions and other [[mental states]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Levinson|2005|p=5}} | {{harvnb|Bunnin|Yu|2004|pp=52–53}} | {{harvnb|Adajian|2024|loc=§ 2. Definitions From the History of Philosophy}} | {{harvnb|Levinson|2005|p=5}} }}</ref>

[[Conventionalism|Conventionalist]] definitions view art as a [[socially constructed]] category. This means that it does not primarily depend on the inherent properties of objects, for example, what they represent or what forms they have. Instead, art is defined by social and cultural agreements, which are subject to change. A key motivation for this approach has been the emergence of modern art, which has challenged many earlier conceptions. Conventionalist definitions can explain, for instance, that even mundane [[Found object|ready-made objects]] like [[Fountain (Duchamp)|a urinal]] are considered art if conventions say so. Institutional theories argue that the conventions are set by social institutions of the [[art world]]. Because of this social dependence, an object considered art in one [[society]] may not be art in another society. Historical theories, another form of conventionalism, assert that the category of art depends on established traditions and historical contexts. They claim that an object becomes part of this category if it stands in the right relation to these traditions, for example, by being created in an artistic context and resembling other recognized artworks.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Adajian|2024|loc=Lead section, § 4. Contemporary Definitions}} | {{harvnb|Davies|2013|pp=215–217}} | {{harvnb|Bunnin|Yu|2004|pp=52–53, 350}} | {{harvnb|Beauchamp|2005|p=15}} | {{harvnb|Levinson|2005|p=14}} }}</ref>

There are also hybrid theories that combine elements from other theories. For instance, one approach holds that an object is an artwork if it either meets certain aesthetic standards or is conventionally regarded as art.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Adajian|2024|loc=§ 4.5 Hybrid (Disjunctive) Definitions}} | {{harvnb|Davies|2013|pp=218–219}} | {{harvnb|Levinson|2005|p=15}} }}</ref> The diversity of proposed definitions{{efn|One classification divides characterizations of art into functional and procedural definitions based on whether they focus on the role of artworks or the rules and procedures used to create and interpret them.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Adajian|2024a|loc=§ 1.}} | {{harvnb|Levinson|2005|p=15}} | {{harvnb|Stecker|2010|pp=120–121}} }}</ref> Another classification distinguishes between essentialist, contextualist, and constructivist conceptions, which emphasize intrinsic features, circumstances of origin, or interpretational practices, respectively.<ref>{{harvnb|Stecker|2010|pp=10–11}}</ref>}} and the difficulties in reconciling them have led some philosophers to argue against the existence of precise criteria. Some conclude that a definition is strictly impossible. Others provide vague characterizations, suggesting that the domain of art is characterized by overlapping similarities, known as [[family resemblance]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Adajian|2024|loc=§ 3. Skepticism About Definitions}} | {{harvnb|Beauchamp|2005|p=15}} | {{harvnb|Stecker|2010|pp=8, 120–121}} | {{harvnb|Levinson|2005|p=13}} | {{harvnb|Davies|2013|pp=213–215}} }}</ref>

=== Ontology and categories ===
The [[ontology]] of art seeks to discern the fundamental [[categories of being]] to which all artworks belong.{{efn|This inquiry is closely related to definitions of art but not identical, since artworks may belong to the same ontological category as other things. Definitions, by contrast, usually seek to identify features that distinguish artworks from all other things.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Thomasson|2004|p=78}} | {{harvnb|Stecker|2010|pp=8–9}} }}</ref>}} One approach argues that artworks are [[Universal (metaphysics)|universals]]{{em dash}}general or repeatable entities that can have several instances at the same time. For example, a novel can have many copies, a film can have many screenings, and a photo can have many prints. One version of this view distinguishes artworks as [[Type–token distinction|types]] from their instances, which are considered tokens of this type. A different outlook rejects the idea that artworks are universals, arguing instead that they are [[particular]]s or unique concrete entities. For them, if there are several instances, then the artwork is the collection or sum of all instances. According to this view, [[Alfred Stieglitz]]'s photograph ''[[The Steerage]]'' is not a type underlying its prints but rather the collection or sum of all prints together.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Rohrbaugh|2013|pp=235–243}} | {{harvnb|Slater|loc=§ 9. Art Objects}} | {{harvnb|Thomasson|2004|pp=78–83}} }}</ref>

A similar discussion addresses whether artworks are [[material objects]], which exist independent of observers, or [[intentional objects]], which exist in the experience of observers.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Stecker|2010|pp=123–124, 127, 140–141}} | {{harvnb|Munro|Scruton|2025|loc=§ The Aesthetic Object}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=11–13}} | {{harvnb|Thomasson|2004|pp=78–81}} | {{harvnb|Beauchamp|2005|p=15}} }}</ref> Pluralists argue that different types of artworks belong to distinct ontological categories.{{efn|For example, [[Richard Wollheim]] and [[Nicholas Wolterstorff]] hold that some artworks, such as paintings, are physical objects, while others have a non-physical nature, such as literature.<ref>{{harvnb|Thomasson|2004|pp=82–83}}</ref> [[Noël Carroll]] argues that [[mass art]], which can be delivered to many people in distinct locations at the same time, belongs to a different ontological category than other forms of art.<ref>{{harvnb|Davies|2005|p=161}}</ref>}} Contextualists accept this view and further propose that the ontological category depends on the context of discussion.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Stecker|2010|pp=131–132, 140–141}} | {{harvnb|Thomasson|2004|pp=78–79}} }}</ref> Deflationism is skeptical about the fundamental existence of artworks in any form. It acknowledges that the term ''art'' may be practically useful in everyday language but rejects that it refers to any fundamental entities of reality.<ref>{{harvnb|Rohrbaugh|2013|pp=235–243}}</ref>

[[File:OilPaintTube.jpg|thumb|alt=Photo of various tubes of oil paint|Some categorizations of art forms focus on the medium used to express artistic ideas, such as the use of oil paint.<ref name="auto">{{harvnb|Davies|2013a|pp=225–226}}</ref>]]

Artworks are categorized in many ways. Some distinctions focus on the [[Artistic medium|medium]] used to express artistic ideas. For example, paintings typically use [[paint]], such as [[Oil paint|oil]] or [[acrylic paint]], which is distributed on a surface, whereas dance involves bodily movements. Similarly, music is performed using instruments and voice to produce sounds, and literature relies on language. Hybrid forms like [[opera]] and [[film]] combine several of these elements.<ref name="auto"/> Another distinction is between performance works and object works. Performance works, like a song performed on stage, are dynamically enacted in time, whereas object works, like a painting, have a more static nature.<ref>{{harvnb|Slater|loc=§ 9. Art Objects}}</ref> Artworks can also be classified by [[Art history|art historic]] style, such as [[impressionism]] and [[surrealism]], and by their intended purpose, like political and [[religious art]].<ref>{{harvnb|Davies|2013a|pp=225–226, 232–233}}</ref>

=== Meaning ===
The meaning of an artwork is what is involved in understanding it or comprehending what it communicates, encompassing factors such as representation and expression. Certain aspects of meaning may be directly accessible; others require in-depth interpretation, for example, to grasp symbolic or [[metaphor]]ical elements. Understanding influences aesthetic experience, and for certain artworks, a comprehensive understanding may be required to fully appreciate them.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Stecker|2010|pp=9–10, 163}} | {{harvnb|Munro|Scruton|2025|loc=§ Understanding Art, § Representation and Expression in Art}} }}</ref> One approach to the analysis of meaning is the distinction between [[form and content]]. Content refers to what is presented, such as the depicted topic, expressed ideas, and conceptual messages. Form refers to how the content is presented, such as medium, technique, composition, and [[art style|style]]. Form encompasses modes of presentation in different art forms, like color and spatial arrangement in painting, [[harmony]] and [[rhythm]] in music, and [[narrative voice]] and plot structure in literature.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|p=126}} | {{harvnb|Munro|Scruton|2025|loc=§ Relationship Between Form and Content}} }}</ref>

==== Representation and expression ====
[[File:Edvard Munch - The Scream - Google Art Project.jpg|thumb|upright=.8|alt=Oil painting of a person screaming against the backdrop of an orange sky|The emotions artworks express are a central topic in the philosophy of art, such as the feelings of [[Social alienation|alienation]] and [[existential dread]] in [[Edvard Munch]]'s 1893 painting ''[[The Scream]]''.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Ridley|2005|pp=212–213}} | {{harvnb|Kraut|2023|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=mZXTEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA285 285]}} }}</ref>]]

[[Representation (arts)|Representation]] is a depiction of real or imagined entities. For example, a [[portrait]] painting represents a person, and a [[fantasy novel]] represents an imaginary chain of events. Similarity is a crucial element in many forms of artistic representation, meaning that the artwork resembles the depicted entity. Representation can also happen through other means, such as conventional [[symbol]]s and established codes. It is particularly prevalent in certain art forms and styles, such as [[classical art]] and [[Realism (arts)|realism]]. Since [[Ancient history|antiquity]], representation has been a key concept in [[Theory of art|theories of art]], such as Plato's idea of defining art as imitation. However, it is controversial whether representation plays a central role in all art forms, including music{{efn|According to one proposal, music uses tempo, tone, and volume to represent emotions.<ref>{{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=268–269}}</ref>}} and [[Abstract art|abstract modern art]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Goldman|2005|pp=192–193, 196–197}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=268–269}} }}</ref>

Expression is the conveyance of psychological states, such as [[emotions]], [[Mood (psychology)|moods]], and attitudes. For example, a painter may depict a barren landscape in muted colors to express [[sadness]], and a musician might use a fast tempo and upbeat melody to convey excitement. The expressed mental states often align with the artist's personal experience. However, this is not necessarily the case, and artists may explore psychological states they observed in others or entirely fictional experiences. An artwork can express a mental state like sadness by evoking it in the experience of the audience. Alternatively, the expression can also happen if observers recognize the presence of sadness in the artwork even if they do not personally feel it. Expression theories consider expression a core feature of artworks. They characterize artworks as expressions of the artist's mind, focusing on [[creativity]] and [[originality]] in the manifestation of aesthetic experiences.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Stecker|2010|pp=201–205}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=113–114}} | {{harvnb|Ridley|2005|pp=211–213}} }}</ref>

==== Interpretation and criticism ====
[[File:Las Meninas, by Diego Velázquez, from Prado in Google Earth.jpg|thumb|upright=0.7|alt=Painting of a large room with several people, including a girl in a white dress at the center|Interpretation seeks to uncover the meaning of artworks, such as the significance of the canvas and mirror shown in [[Diego Velázquez]]'s 1656 painting ''[[Las Meninas]]''.<ref name="auto15"/>]]
The process of [[Aesthetic interpretation|interpretation]] is the attempt to uncover{{efn|An alternative view suggests that interpretation does not uncover meaning but creates it.<ref>{{harvnb|Currie|2005|pp=291–292}}</ref>}} the meaning of an artwork to understand its significance and value. In the widest sense, interpretation encompasses any way of assigning [[Meaning (philosophy)|meaning]], including obvious descriptions of depicted entities and explanations of [[Literal and figurative language|literal word meanings]]. In philosophy of art, the term is typically used in a narrower sense for assignments of meaning that involve deeper analysis and creative thought, such as the examination of the canvas and mirror shown in [[Diego Velázquez]]'s 1656 painting ''[[Las Meninas]]'' to explore the relation between painter, viewer, and depicted topic. Interpretations aim to discover underlying aspects that are relevant to the understanding and appreciation of the artwork.<ref name="auto15">{{multiref | {{harvnb|Stecker|2013|pp=10, 309–310}} | {{harvnb|Currie|2005|pp=291–292}} | {{harvnb|Walton|2016|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=cBoTDQAAQBAJ&pg=PA37 37]}} | {{harvnb|Shapiro|2003|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=9swA8bl8tR4C&pg=PA251 251]}}}}</ref> The terms ''interpretation'' and ''[[art criticism|criticism]]'' are sometimes used interchangeably. However, criticism is typically associated with more components, like a general description of the criticized artwork and a classification of style and [[genre]]. Criticism also explains the art-historical background and evaluates positive and negative qualities.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=80–82}} | {{harvnb|Gilmore|2013|pp=375–376}} }}</ref>

Critics sometimes propose conflicting interpretations of the same artwork. According to critical monism, there is only one comprehensive correct interpretation, implying that conflicting interpretations cannot both be correct. Critical pluralism, by contrast, asserts that there can be different but equally valid interpretations and that it is not always possible to determine which of two conflicting interpretations is superior. A similar debate addresses whether interpretations can be true or false in an objective sense.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Currie|2005|pp=292–293}} | {{harvnb|Stecker|2010|p=306}} | {{harvnb|Stecker|2013|p=314}} }}</ref>

Several frameworks of interpretation have been proposed. According to [[authorial intentionalism|intentionalism]], the meaning of an artwork is determined by the author's intent{{em dash}}their reasons and motives that led to the creation of the artwork.{{efn|Intentionalism focuses on the author's original intent rather than their retrospective interpretation, which can overlap but are not necessarily identical.<ref>{{harvnb|Stecker|2013|pp=310–311}}</ref>}} This typically involves analyzing the ideas the artist aimed to express but can also include a [[biographical]] analysis to learn about psychological and social circumstances in the artist's life.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Currie|2005|pp=294–295}} | {{harvnb|Stecker|2013|pp=310–311}} }}</ref>

Intentionalism is a controversial theory, termed the ''intentional fallacy'' by its critics. Some objections point to cases where the author's intention cannot be known, where the author  cannot be identified, or where no traditional author exists, as in artworks created by [[artificial intelligence]]. In these cases, meaning would be inaccessible or non-existent.{{efn|As a result, some theorists follow [[Roland Barthes]] in talking about "[[the death of the author]]" to emphasize the artwork itself rather than its origin.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Beauchamp|2005|p=15}} | {{harvnb|Janaway|2005c}} }}</ref>}} Other objections assert that an artist may fail to accurately express their intention or may manifest unintended aesthetic features, suggesting that an artwork can contain both less and more than the artist intended.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Stecker|2013|pp=311–312}} | {{harvnb|Currie|2005|pp=294–296, 298}} | {{harvnb|Beauchamp|2005|p=15}} }}</ref>

An alternative to intentionalism argues that meaning is determined by artistic, stylistic, linguistic, and other cultural [[Convention (norm)|conventions]]. For example, linguistic conventions determine the literal meanings of words and thereby influence the overall meaning of a poem. Another framework holds that meaning is shaped by how the audience, rather than the author, interprets or would interpret the intention underlying the work.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Stecker|2013|pp=315–316}} | {{harvnb|Currie|2005|pp=294–296}} }}</ref> Artistic formalism proposes a different approach by focusing interpretation exclusively on formal or perceptual features of artworks.<ref>{{harvnb|Shelley|2022|loc=§ 2.1 Aesthetic Objects, 2.5.1 The Aesthetic Question}}</ref>

Aestheticism and instrumentalism are theories about the value of art. Aestheticism asserts that the primary value of art lies in its intrinsic aesthetic merits, independent of any external purposes. This idea of the autonomy of art is expressed in the slogan "[[art for art's sake]]". Strong forms of aestheticism not only disregard external purposes but see them as detrimental influences that undermine artistic integrity. Instrumentalism, by contrast, explains the value of art by the effects it has on other domains. It understands art as a means to things such as [[moral education]], [[spiritual growth]], [[therapeutic]] benefits, and [[social cohesion]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Janaway|2005b}} | {{harvnb|Bunnin|Yu|2004|pp=15, 17, 52–53}} | {{harvnb|Beauchamp|2005|pp=14–15}} }}</ref>

=== The individual arts ===
{{main|The arts}}
The individual arts are practices or disciplines in the domain of art. They encompass a wide range of fields, including traditionally established forms such as painting, music, and literature, as well as newer types like [[Video games as an art form|video games]].<ref>{{harvnb|Graham|2005|pp=1–2}}</ref> One classification divides them into [[visual arts]], [[literary arts]], and [[performance arts]]. The boundaries between these categories are not always clear, and alternative classifications have been proposed.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Poole|Scott|2021|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Ix4nEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA383 383]}} | {{harvnb|Graham|2005|p=76}} }}</ref>

[[File:West African Dance at the White House, 2007Apr25.jpg|thumb|alt=Photo of dancing African women|Dance is a performance art involving a series of bodily movements.<ref name="auto2">{{multiref | {{harvnb|McFee|2013|pp=649–650}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=84–85}} }}</ref>]]

[[Painting]] is a visual art in which a painter applies colors to a surface. It allows for a diverse range of motives and styles, and is often considered a paradigm form of art.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=232–233}} | {{harvnb|Graham|2005|pp=151–153}} | {{harvnb|McIver Lopes|2013|pp=596–597}} }}</ref> The representation of real entities plays a central role in many forms of painting, ranging from landscapes and people to historic events. This process involves artistic choices that go beyond simple replication, such as guiding the viewer's attention to specific aspects or highlighting important but easily overlooked features.<ref>{{harvnb|McIver Lopes|2013|pp=596–597}}</ref> The issue of representation is also crucial in [[photography]], a visual art shaped by technological developments in [[camera]] design and [[Image editing|editing]] processes. A key topic in the philosophy of photography concerns its mechanical manner of authentically representing real objects, frequently drawing parallels and distinctions with painting. The status of photographs as true artworks is disputed, with critics arguing that the mechanical nature of capturing images lacks the necessary artistic creativity.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Wilson|2013|pp=585–590}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=241–243}} }}</ref>

[[Music]] is a performance art in which sounds are combined to create aesthetic patterns, relying on aspects such as [[melody]] and rhythm. Unlike painting and photography, it is typically less associated with objective representation and more closely linked to the expression of emotions.{{efn|Formalists downplay the focus on expressive qualities, such as [[Eduard Hanslick]], who argues that music is primarily a progression of sounds rather than an emotional story.<ref>{{harvnb|Townsend|2006|p=141}}</ref> [[Susanne K. Langer]] sought to establish a connection between the emotional and symbolic dimensions of music, asserting that musical forms are symbols that convey the artist's knowledge of feeling but have no conventionally fixed meanings.<ref>{{harvnb|Windle|loc=§ 5. Theory of Art}}</ref>}} A key discussion in the [[philosophy of music]] concerns the [[definition of music]] or the criteria under which a combination of sounds qualifies as music. Proposals range from objective criteria, such as the patterns of how sounds are organized, to subjective criteria, focusing on audience experience and interpretation.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Kania|2013|pp=639–640}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=213–215}} }}</ref> [[Dance]] is another performance art in which dancers create aesthetic patterns through a series of bodily movements, often following a [[choreography]]. It is typically accompanied by music and shares with music an emphasis on expressive features.<ref name="auto2"/>

[[File:Σαγράδα Φαμίλια 2941.jpg|thumb|upright=.7|alt=Photo of the Sagrada Família, a cathedral with tall, intricate towers and detailed facades|Architecture is an art that typically combines aesthetic with functional goals, such as [[Antoni Gaudí]]'s [[Sagrada Família]].<ref name="auto12">{{multiref | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=26–28}} | {{harvnb|Winters|2013|pp=627–638}} }}</ref>]]

[[Architecture]] is the art or craft of designing and building, encompassing a wide range of structures from [[monument]]s and [[cathedral]]s to [[skyscraper]]s and residential homes. It typically combines aesthetic with functional goals, seeking to create buildings that are both visually appealing and practically useful. This dual nature is a central topic of the [[philosophy of architecture]], with one theory suggesting that mere buildings can be distinguished from artistic architecture by the presence of [[ornament (art)|decorative elements]].<ref name="auto12"/> [[Sculpture]] is another art form that, like architecture, involves the creation of three-dimensional works. Sculptures are usually static objects made of robust materials like stone, metal, and wood, but may also include dynamic elements, as is the case for [[Kinetic art|kinetic sculptures]]. Key discussions in the philosophy of sculpture address the definition, representational aspects, and aesthetic features of sculptures as well as the influence of the chosen material.<ref>{{harvnb|Irvin|2013|pp=606–607, 613–614}}</ref>

Literature has language as its primary medium. In its widest sense, literature encompasses any written document. However, the term is typically used in a narrower sense in aesthetics for forms of writing that belong to the [[high art]]s, such as [[poetry|poems]], [[novel]]s, and [[drama]]. Literature as an art is often characterized by its deliberate, elaborate, and organized use of language, but there is no universally accepted demarcation between artistic literature and other forms of writing.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Lamarque|2013|pp=521–523}} | {{harvnb|Livingston|2005|pp=536–538}} }}</ref> Poetry is a distinct form of literature often written in [[Verse (poetry)|verses]] composed of several lines that may follow specific patterns, such as [[Metre (poetry)|meter]] and [[rhyme]]. Many poems are characterized by an economical use of language that seeks to evoke specific experiences while being difficult to [[paraphrase]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Neill|2005|pp=605–606}} | {{harvnb|Lamarque|2013a|pp=532–536}} }}</ref>

[[Theater]] is a performance art that combines elements from other art forms. It typically includes a carefully prepared set or stage where actors perform, usually incorporating storytelling and sound design to create immersive experiences. Theater is performed before a live audience, which can create a sense of immediacy that is less prevalent in related art forms, such as film.<ref>{{harvnb|Hamilton|2013|pp=543, 546–547, 549–550}}</ref> [[Film]] also integrates aspects from several artistic disciplines but relies more heavily on technological means of recording and editing. Films can involve actors but may also include [[animated film|animated]] characters or [[documentary|document]] real-life events. They are normally the result of collaborative efforts of many people, which complicates the identification of a singular author in the traditional sense.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=120–121}} | {{harvnb|Graham|2005|pp=116–117}} | {{harvnb|Wartenberg|2025|loc=§ 3. Film and Authorship}} }}</ref>

[[Video game]]s are a more recent form of art. Like theater and film, they usually blend visual, auditory, and narrative elements. They typically stand out through their emphasis on player interaction, allowing active exploration of and engagement with the [[Virtual world|game world]].<ref name="auto5">{{harvnb|Tavinor|2009|pp=1–2, 11–12, 29–30, 172–173, 196}}</ref> The status of films and video games as serious forms of art is disputed. Proponents tend to emphasize their aesthetic qualities; critics often point to their association with [[mass production]] and [[popular culture]] as counterarguments.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Tavinor|2009|pp=1–2, 11–12, 29–30, 172–173, 196}} | {{harvnb|Carroll|1998|pp=185–186}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=120–121}} | {{harvnb|Wartenberg|2025|loc=§ 2. The Nature of Film}} }}</ref> For video games, a related debate centers on the elements of competition and winning, questioning whether these elements run counter to the spirit of art.<ref name="auto5"/>

== In various fields ==
Aesthetic phenomena are investigated in several fields. Some areas examine the relationship between aesthetics and other branches of philosophy or compare different artistic traditions; others study aesthetic elements in everyday life or engage in scientific inquiry using [[Empirical research|empirical methods]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Shimamura|2012|pp=3–4, 14–15, 19–20}} | {{harvnb|Kivy|2004|pp=7, 10–11}} }}</ref>{{efn|The term ''[[applied aesthetics]]'' is sometimes used for attempts to apply general aesthetic principles to specific areas or practices, such as environmental and everyday aesthetics.<ref>{{harvnb|Davies|2016|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=IYqwDQAAQBAJ&pg=PA487 487–488, 490–493, 498]}}</ref>}}

=== Ethics ===
[[Ethics]] is the branch of philosophy that studies [[Morality|moral phenomena]] in general and right [[Action (philosophy)|behavior]] in particular. Artworks can have ethical consequences by influencing how people feel, perceive, and evaluate their circumstances. For example, artworks can glorify violence and reinforce biases, just as they can inspire empathy and challenge societal norms. As a result, art is also relevant to the field of politics since it can steer political sentiment to legitimize authority or mobilize resistance, thereby influencing voter attitudes. Artworks can also explore morally relevant topics without expressing a clear positive or negative evaluation, such as a novel examining an [[ethical dilemma]] without favoring one solution over the others.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Stecker|2010|pp=105, 229, 248–249, 253–254, 262}} | {{harvnb|Hepburn|2005}} | {{harvnb|Norman|2005|p=622}} | {{harvnb|Williams|1993|loc=[https://books.google.com/books?id=_FG0O_M-mHEC&pg=PA237 237]}}}}</ref>

Since both ethics and aesthetics [[Value theory|deal with values]], philosophers seek to clarify the relationship between moral and aesthetic values, proposing several theories of their interaction.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Levinson|2005a}} | {{harvnb|Rodríguez|José|2012|pp=62–67}} | {{harvnb|Tanner|1998|loc=Lead section, § 1. Origins of the Discussion}} }}</ref> Ethicism asserts that the moral value of an artwork can increase its aesthetic value, while ethical defects may undermine its [[artistic merit]]. This view is reversed by immoralism, which suggests that in some cases, moral flaws enhance aesthetic experience. Autonomism rejects both positions, arguing that these domains of evaluation are independent.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Stecker|2010|pp=255–257, 305–307}} | {{harvnb|Hepburn|2005}} | {{harvnb|Peek|loc=Lead section}} }}</ref>

=== Psychology and related fields ===
Scientific approaches rooted in [[psychology]] and related fields employ empirical methods to conduct inquiries and justify hypotheses.<ref>{{harvnb|Shimamura|2012|pp=3–4, 14–15, 19–20}}</ref> The [[Psychology of art|psychology of aesthetics]] examines the mental processes involved in the perception and appreciation of beauty and art, using methods such as [[experimentation]], [[observation]], and [[Survey (human research)|surveys]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Dumont|2008|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=MP5X2SK2DCgC&pg=PA17 17, 27–30, 48]}} | {{harvnb|Lindauer|2011|pp=58–59}} | {{harvnb|Locher|2012|pp=163–165}} }}</ref>

[[Experimental aesthetics]] is an early and influential approach pioneered by [[Gustav Fechner]]. It follows a bottom-up [[methodology]] that starts with human [[Sense|sensation]], investigating preferences to simple physical stimuli, such as basic colors and shapes.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Shimamura|2012|pp=14–16}} | {{harvnb|Mikalonytė|Doran|Liao|2024|loc=§ 1. History of Empirical Research on Art and Aesthetics}} }}</ref> [[Gestalt psychology]] relies on a more holistic outlook, examining how composition and object placement influence aesthetic experience, like the relationship between balanced organization and a sense of calm. Some works, such as [[Daniel Berlyne]]'s approach, shift the focus from perception to emotion, suggesting that features like novelty and complexity cause arousal and that the right amount of arousal is pleasurable.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Shimamura|2012|pp=14–16}} | {{harvnb|Lindauer|2011|pp=58–59}} }}</ref>

Psychological analysis also examines the temporal structure of aesthetic experiences of art. One outlook identifies two phases: an initial impression in which the observer forms a rough general idea of the artwork's topic, structure, and meaning, followed by a focal analysis of more specific features.<ref>{{harvnb|Locher|2012|pp=164, 173, 175}}</ref> Research further explores how circumstances influence aesthetic experience, like the contrast between encountering a painting in a museum or a shopping mall. Along with physical circumstances, social and personal factors also influence aesthetic experience, such as [[group dynamics]], prior knowledge, and the [[motivation]] for seeking the experience.<ref>{{harvnb|Locher|2012|pp=181–183}}</ref>

[[File:Rangeland with grass and bush vegetation in Namibia (3).jpg|thumb|alt=Photo of a landscape with grass, trees, and a blue sky with clouds|Evolutionary psychology examines the evolutionary function of aesthetic sensitivities, like preferences for environments conducive to survival, such as landscapes resembling the African [[savanna]].<ref name="auto3">{{harvnb|Dutton|2005|pp=693–695}}</ref>]]

[[Evolutionary psychology]] analyzes [[mental phenomena]] as products of [[natural selection]]. It asserts that [[genetic variations]] responsible for new capacities are passed on to future generations if they enhance [[Survival of the fittest|survival and reproduction]]. Adopting this approach, [[evolutionary aesthetics]] interprets beauty and other aesthetic experiences as adaptive traits that guide fitness-relevant preferences.<ref>{{harvnb|Dutton|2005|pp=695–696}}</ref> Examples are aesthetic preferences for environments conducive to survival, such as landscapes resembling the African [[savanna]], and [[sexual selection]] by identifying genetically fit mates.<ref>{{harvnb|Dutton|2005|pp=697–700}}</ref> By focusing on the relatively permanent biological nature of humans, evolutionary psychology sees aesthetic values as universal or transcultural patterns of taste and appreciation, contrasting with subjectivist theories that understand aesthetic values as cultural constructs.<ref name="auto3"/>

[[Neuroaesthetics]] applies [[neuroscientific]] insights and methods to study the relationship between brain activity and aesthetic experience. Aesthetic experiences arise from brain processes responsible for organizing sensory stimuli, forming cognitive interpretations, and generating emotional responses. Neuroaesthetics examines these processes using empirical methods, including [[neuroimaging]] techniques like [[fMRI]]. In one type of experiment, participants view artworks, some considered beautiful and others ugly, with researchers noting that the brain area known as the [[orbitofrontal cortex]] is more active when viewing beautiful paintings.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Shimamura|2012|pp=19–22}} | {{harvnb|Chatterjee|2012|pp=299–302}} }}</ref>

[[Cognitive science]], another field, employs an interdisciplinary approach to study mental phenomena by examining how they access and transform [[information]]. An influential theory, suggested by [[Ernst Gombrich]], analyzes aesthetic experience through the interplay of low-level and high-level information processes: sensory processes provide low-level information, which is organized and interpreted using high-level conceptual background knowledge.<ref>{{harvnb|Shimamura|2012|pp=16–18}}</ref> Another approach analyzes aesthetic representation through the [[modularity of mind]]{{em dash}}the hypothesis that the mind is composed of mental modules that function independently. It argues that paintings represent real objects by triggering the same mental modules responsible for the [[Object recognition|recognition of those objects]].<ref>{{harvnb|Stokes|2009|pp=715, 722–724}}</ref>

=== Comparative aesthetics ===
Comparative aesthetics examines diverse aesthetic traditions, analyzing the similarities and differences in their standards of beauty and theoretical approaches.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Deutsch|1998|pp=409–410}} | {{harvnb|Higgins|2005|pp=679–680}} | {{harvnb|Bahm|1965|pp=109–110}} }}</ref> For example, the focus in [[Western culture|Western]] aesthetics on high art and its separation from everyday affairs is not common in most other traditions, for which art is typically closely integrated with practical functions in everyday life, including religion and [[moral education]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Deutsch|1998|pp=409–410}} | {{harvnb|Higgins|2005|pp=679–682, 685–687}} }}</ref> Artistic differences between different traditions also encompass dominant media, common styles, and chosen motifs.<ref name="auto7">{{harvnb|Deutsch|1998|pp=409–410}}</ref>

The comparison of cultural products from different traditions presents conceptual challenges associated with tradition-specific aesthetic concepts and standards of evaluation. The uncritical application of standards from one tradition to evaluate the works of another can result in [[cultural imperialism]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Deutsch|1998|pp=409–410}} | {{harvnb|Higgins|2005|pp=680–681}} }}</ref> At the same time, these differences provide opportunities to artists and philosophers to incorporate new elements and explore novel perspectives.<ref name="auto7"/>

[[Indian aesthetics]] draws a close connection between artistic activity and religious practice. It argues that artistic expression is a [[Spirituality|spiritual]] endeavor that should be informed by knowledge of the [[Ātman (Hinduism)|self]] and [[Brahman|reality]], express [[Bhakti|devotion to the divine]], and [[Nishkama Karma|avoid attachments to the fruits of the activity]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Deutsch|1998|pp=410–411}} | {{harvnb|Higgins|2005|pp=681–682}} }}</ref> Traditional Indian aesthetics analyzes art in terms of basic life emotions, called [[Rasa (aesthetics)|rasas]], such as delight, humor, sadness, and anger. It sees art as a [[Lila (Hinduism)|play]] that imitates reality by conveying experiences of the rasas. Its focus is on the universal expressions of human emotional life rather than person-specific feelings. This school of thought identifies artistic creativity as the ability to harness the full potential of the medium, like colors, sounds, and words, to convey experiential universals. For the audience, it recommends an aesthetic attitude characterized by a psychic distance from private concerns to transcend the personal self and become receptive to universal elements.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Deutsch|1998|pp=410–411}} | {{harvnb|Higgins|2005|p=681}} | {{harvnb|Chandran|Sreenath|2021|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=9ChOEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA33 33–35]}} | {{harvnb|Bhirdikar|2020}} }}</ref>

[[File:Landscape after Night Rain Shower.jpg|thumb|upright=.8|alt=Painting of a hilly landscape together with poetry in the top right area|[[Chinese aesthetics]] places specific emphasis on [[poetry]], [[painting]], and [[calligraphy]]. They are known as the [[three perfections]] and are sometimes combined in a single artwork, as in [[Kun Can]]'s ''Landscape after Night Rain Shower''.<ref>{{harvnb|Goldberg|1998|loc=Lead section}}</ref>]]

[[Chinese aesthetics]] emphasizes the spontaneous nature of artistic creativity and its connection to the moral and spiritual domains. It argues that art should foster harmony within society and align with the [[Dao|natural order of the universe]]. In this role, art is both self-expression and [[self-cultivation]] aimed at promoting social well-being.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Deutsch|1998|pp=409–410}} | {{harvnb|Higgins|2005|p=685}} | {{harvnb|Goldberg|1998|loc=Lead section}} }}</ref> The main focus of Chinese aesthetics is on poetry, painting, and [[calligraphy]], known as the [[three perfections]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Goldberg|1998|loc=Lead section}} | {{harvnb|Peng|2025|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=LYFDEQAAQBAJ&pg=PR31 xxxi]}} | {{harvnb|Li|2022|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=WJlXEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA149 149–150]}} }}</ref> This tradition influenced [[Japanese aesthetics]], which is characterized by its interest in nature. Different art styles in this tradition are shaped by religious outlooks, particularly [[Shinto]] and [[Buddhism]]. Japanese theories of art stress the interrelation between the experience of the artist and the response of the audience.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Viswanathan|1998|loc=Lead section}} | {{harvnb|Higgins|2005|pp=682–683}} }}</ref>

[[Islamic philosophy|Islamic philosophers]] see art as a means of communicating philosophical and religious truths, making them accessible to the general public without requiring abstract theoretical thought. Thinkers such as [[Al-Farabi]] and [[Avicenna]] argued that imagination rather than reasoning underlies artistic creation and appreciation. According to this view, art imitates reality and evokes emotions to convey underlying truths and positively influence behavior.<ref>{{harvnb|Black|1998|loc=Lead section, § 3. Imitation and Imagination}}</ref> Religious teachings play a central role in Islamic aesthetics. For example, the belief that [[Allah]] is transcendent and boundless has resulted in the [[Aniconism in Islam|avoidance of figurative depictions]] and the emphasis on [[Islamic geometric patterns|abstract art forms]].<ref name="auto14">{{harvnb|Higgins|2005|pp=681–682}}</ref>{{efn|This influence can be seen in abstract patterns used in Islamic art, such as a single line that curls back into itself to represent Allah's unity and omnipresence.<ref name="auto14"/>}}

African aesthetics emphasizes the intuitive and emotional nature of art, highlighting its communal function in social life. Early scholarship on this tradition was typically conducted from an [[ethnocentric]] perspective using Western aesthetic standards to interpret and evaluate African art. This usually resulted in the portrayal of African artworks as exotic curiosities that lack the sophistication of high art. The emergence of [[Indigenous science|indigenous scholarship]] in the 20th century sought to correct this interpretation, arguing that the emphasis on moral, emotional, and intuitive aspects reflects different artistic standards rather than a deficiency. This school of thought, often associated with the concept of [[Négritude]], focuses on the importance of feelings in contrast to abstraction and intellectual analysis.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Hallen|1998|loc=Lead section, § 1. Primitive Cultures and Négritude}} | {{harvnb|Hallen|1998a|pp=37–38}} }}</ref>

=== Environment, everyday life, and religion ===
[[Aesthetics of nature|Environmental aesthetics]] deals with the appreciation of nature, including elements such as forests, mountain ranges, rivers, and flowers.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Carlson|2013|pp=485–489}} | {{harvnb|Stecker|2010|pp=15–18}} | {{harvnb|Crawford|2004|pp=306–307}} }}</ref> It encompasses both transient appearances, such as the fleeting beauty of a landscape during sunset, and enduring aspects, such as the majesty of a centuries-old tree.<ref>{{harvnb|Stecker|2010|pp=15–25}}</ref> This field focuses on sensory and formal qualities associated with beauty and related aesthetic qualities. In this respect, it contrasts with the philosophy of art, which typically emphasizes the interpretation of underlying meanings associated with expression and representation.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Carlson|2013|pp=485–489}} | {{harvnb|Stecker|2010|pp=15–18}} | {{harvnb|Crawford|2004|pp=306–310}} | {{harvnb|Fisher|2005|pp=668–669}} }}</ref> Some approaches to environmental aesthetics also consider the impact of background knowledge on the aesthetic experience of nature. For instance, [[ecological]] awareness of the intricate relationships within an [[ecosystem]] can shape the appreciation of a [[woodland]] environment by understanding it as a [[habitat]] of diverse species.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Carlson|2013|p=490}} | {{harvnb|Stecker|2010|pp=25–28}} }}</ref>

[[File:Large Buddha Statue in Buddha Park, Ravangla.jpg|thumb|alt=Photo of a golden Buddha statue|Religious art serves specific religious functions, such as conveying moral teachings or aiding devotional practices.<ref name="auto6">{{multiref | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=267–268}} | {{harvnb|Wolterstorff|2004|pp=325–328, 338}} | {{harvnb|Graham|2013|pp=509–510}} }}</ref>]]

In its broadest sense, environmental aesthetics encompasses the appreciation of any environment, including those created by humans.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Carlson|2013|pp=485–486}} | {{harvnb|Stecker|2010|pp=15–16}} | {{harvnb|Fisher|2005|pp=667–668}} }}</ref> This inquiry is closely associated with [[Everyday Aesthetics|everyday aesthetics]], which examines aesthetic phenomena encountered in daily life. Everyday aesthetics covers both public and private environments, ranging from modern cities and industrial sites to private homes and backyards, as well as personal adornments and consumer products, such as clothing, hairstyles, [[industrial design]], and [[web design]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Carlson|2013|pp=492–493}} | {{harvnb|Sartwell|2005|pp=761–762}} }}</ref> The aesthetics of [[popular art]], a related discipline, investigates aesthetic qualities in popular culture and compares the evaluative standards of popular art with those of high or [[fine art]]. For example, it studies the contrast between commercial mass art and experimental [[avant-garde]] and explores specific types of popular art, such as [[kitsch]].<ref>{{harvnb|Novitz|2005|pp=733–735, 737}}</ref>

Art plays a central role in the field of [[religion]] and manifests in [[Religious art|many forms]], including paintings, sculptures, [[Sacral architecture|architecture]], [[Religious music|music]], [[Sacred dance|dance]], and literature. Its key characteristic comes from its religious function, such as conveying [[theology|theological]] and moral teachings, representing symbolic truths, inspiring religious experiences, and aiding devotional practices.{{efn|[[Theological aesthetics]] studies how beauty and art reveal the divine and shape the understanding of religion.<ref>{{harvnb|Viladesau|1999|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Ys_nCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA11 11–12]}}</ref>}} Religious art is part of all [[World religion|major religions]] and was the dominant art form during [[Ancient period|ancient]] and [[Medieval period|medieval times]]. Its influence began to wane in the [[modern period]] due to [[secularization]]. This shift is also reflected in developments in the philosophy of art that introduced a focus on disinterestedness and the autonomy of aesthetic experience from external purposes, including religious goals.<ref name="auto6"/>

=== Others ===
Several theories of aesthetics are associated with specific philosophical schools of thought. [[Marxist aesthetics]] examines the relationship between art, [[class structure]], and [[Ideology#Marxist interpretation|social ideology]], exploring how art can enforce or challenge established power hierarchies.<ref>{{harvnb|Munro|Scruton|2025|loc=§ Marxist Aesthetics}}</ref> [[Feminist aesthetics]] criticizes male biases in aesthetic theory and artistic practice while discussing alternatives. It investigates unfair social institutions and aesthetic standards that disadvantage women and exclude them from the art world. An example is the [[male gaze]]{{em dash}}a cultural phenomenon that treats women as objects of male spectatorship rather than as artistic creators.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Korsmeyer|Weiser|2021|loc=Lead section, § 1. Art and Artists: Historical Background, § 3. Aesthetic Categories and Feminist Critiques, § 5. The Body in Art and Philosophy}} | {{harvnb|Argüello Manresa|2019|loc=Lead section, § Feminist Critique of Philosophical Aesthetics, § Feminist Philosophy and Theory of the Arts}} }}</ref> [[Postmodernism|Postmodern]] aesthetics is a diverse movement that challenges established concepts and theories in the field of aesthetics. It typically rejects the focus on disinterested pleasure, the autonomy of art from other domains, and the distinction between high and popular art. It tends to promote a [[Pluralism (philosophy)|pluralism]] that embraces diversity, playfulness, and [[irony]].<ref>{{harvnb|Shusterman|2005|pp=771–772, 781–782}}</ref>

[[File:Mandel zoom 00 mandelbrot set.jpg|thumb|alt=Rendered geometric fractal of a black shape against a blue background|[[Computer art]] includes the generation of images using [[algorithms]], such as the [[fractal geometry]] of the [[Mandelbrot set]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Taylor|2014|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=gVUTAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA165 165]}} | {{harvnb|Binkley|1998|pp=412–413}} }}</ref>]]

The term [[mathematical beauty]] refers to aesthetic qualities of abstract mathematical concepts and theories. For instance, a [[mathematical proof]] may be considered beautiful if it demonstrates a profound insight in an effective manner or reveals an underlying unity of seemingly disparate mathematical ideas.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Cellucci|2017|pp=335–336}} | {{harvnb|Sa|Alcock|Inglis|Tanswell|2024|pp=299–301}} }}</ref> The [[aesthetics of science]] examines aesthetic judgments about scientific theories and practices, including the role of beauty and creativity in the construction of models.<ref>{{harvnb|Ivanova|French|2020|pp=1–5}}</ref>

[[Computer art]] involves the use of computers in the creation of artworks.{{efn|In its broadest sense, computer art refers to any [[digital art]], including artworks that merely reproduce conventional art styles with digital means. In a narrower sense, only artworks with characteristics not commonly associated with other art forms, such as [[interactivity]], are considered computer art.<ref>{{harvnb|Lopes|2009|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=GtuOAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA1 1–3, 21, 26–28]}}</ref>}} It can take many forms, ranging from minor digital enhancements of existing artworks to entirely new creations generated using complex [[algorithm]]s. Its abstract nature, based on symbolic representation and manipulation of electronic signals, distinguishes computer art from traditional forms of art, which rely on more tangible media. This medium offers new artistic possibilities, such as [[virtual reality]] and [[interactivity]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Binkley|1998|pp=412–413}} | {{harvnb|Lopes|2009|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=GtuOAgAAQBAJ&pg=PR11 xi–xii, 1–3, 21, 26–28]}} }}</ref> Rapid developments in [[artificial intelligence]] in the 21st century have significantly impacted computer art. They include the emergence of [[Generative AI|generative models]]{{em dash}}systems that are [[Machine learning|trained]] using existing media to create new texts, images, music, or videos in response to [[Prompt engineering|verbal descriptions of the intended result]]. Examples include [[ChatGPT]], [[Stable Diffusion]], [[MuseNet]], and [[RunwayML]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Jiang|Brown|Cheng|Khan|2023|pp=363–364}} | {{harvnb|Zhou|Lee|2024|loc=§ Introduction}} }}</ref>

Meta-aesthetics examines the fundamental assumptions and concepts underlying aesthetics. It asks about the existence of aesthetic facts, the meaning of aesthetic statements, and the ways of acquiring aesthetic knowledge. A central meta-aesthetic debate between [[Philosophical realism|realism]] and [[anti-realism]] addresses whether there are mind-independent aesthetic facts. A related discussion between [[Cognitivism (ethics)|cognitivism]] and [[non-cognitivism]] considers whether aesthetic statements can be objectively true or primarily [[Emotivism|express personal emotions]].<ref>{{harvnb|King|2023|pp=169–175}}</ref>

== History ==
{{main|History of aesthetics}}

=== Ancient ===
[[File:Plato Silanion Musei Capitolini MC1377.jpg|thumb|upright=.7|alt=Photo of a marble bust of a bearded man|Plato understood art as a [[Techne|craft]] that [[Mimesis|imitates]] reality.<ref name="auto4">{{multiref | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=xvii–xx}} | {{harvnb|Beardsley|2006|pp=41–43}} | {{harvnb|Janaway|2013|pp=3–7}} }}</ref>]]

Aesthetics has its roots in [[Ancient philosophy|ancient thought]], which typically interpreted beauty as a [[metaphysical]] phenomenon associated with the order of the [[cosmos]].<ref>{{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=xvii–xx}}</ref> In [[ancient Greek philosophy]], early explorations of the nature of beauty are found in [[Pythagorean philosophy]] in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE. This tradition proposed that beauty arises from the proportion and harmony between different elements.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Celkyte|loc=Lead section, § 2a. Proportion}} | {{harvnb|Beardsley|2006|pp=41–42}} }}</ref>{{efn|A similar view was later also endorsed by the [[Stoics]].<ref>{{harvnb|Celkyte|loc=Lead section, § 2a. Proportion}}</ref>}} In works like the ''[[Philebus]]'' and ''[[Symposium (Plato)|Symposium]]'', [[Plato]] (427–347 BCE) analyzed pure beauty as an [[Platonic form|immutable form]] that exists independently of matter. He argued that material entities are beautiful if they participate in the form of beauty. Plato understood art as a [[Techne|craft]] that seeks to [[Mimesis|imitate]] and represent material entities. He acknowledged that art has some [[Education|didactic]] value but was overall critical of it, asserting that its derivative nature, based on imitation of sensible features, cannot lead to true knowledge.<ref name="auto4"/>

[[Aristotle]] (384–322 BCE) examined aesthetics through the lens of poetry, providing a detailed analysis in his book ''[[Poetics (Aristotle)|Poetics]]''. He agreed with Plato's idea that art is a form of imitation but adopted a more positive outlook, proposing that it can reveal universal truths. Aristotle suggested that successful artistic imitation is pleasurable and can have therapeutic or [[Catharsis|cathartic]] effects. By linking this pleasure to beauty, he tried to explain why the imitation of unpleasurable phenomena, like [[Tragedy|tragic stories]], can be enjoyable.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Beardsley|2006|pp=43–45}} | {{harvnb|Destrée|2021|loc=Lead section}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|p=xx}} }}</ref> Also influenced by Plato, [[Plotinus]] (204–270 CE) argued that beauty is not based on sensory symmetries or simple proportions but embodies an underlying order, harmony, and unity associated with [[Neoplatonism#The One|the ultimate source of creation]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Spicher ''Medieval Theories''|loc=§1c. Plotinus}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=xx, 248–251}} | {{harvnb|Beardsley|2006|pp=45–46}} }}</ref>

In [[ancient India]], the [[Natya Shastra]], traditionally attributed to [[Bharata (sage)|Bharata]] ({{circa|200 BCE|200 CE}}), formulated the [[Rasa (aesthetics)|rasa theory of art]]. This theory posits that the goal of art is to convey fundamental life emotions as experiential universals of human existence.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Gitomer|1998|p=484}} | {{harvnb|Deutsch|1998|pp=410–411}} | {{harvnb|Higgins|2005|pp=681–682}} }}</ref> In [[ancient China]], the philosophy of art was shaped by [[Confucianism]]. It emphasized [[self-cultivation]] and the relation between nature and human culture.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Goldberg|1998|loc=Lead section, § 1. The Ethico-aesthetic Way of Chinese Art}} | {{harvnb|Saussy|1998|pp=363–364}} }}</ref>

=== Medieval ===
During the [[Medieval aesthetics|medieval period]], the [[Historiography of the Christianization of the Roman Empire|rise of Christianity]] led Western aesthetic thinkers to blend ancient Greek thought with religious teachings, often in the form of philosophical [[theology]].<ref>{{harvnb|Haldane|2013|pp=25–26}}</ref> Influenced by Plato and Plotinus, [[Augustine of Hippo]] (354–430 CE) explored the distinction between artistic creation, which transforms matter, and divine creation, which brings forth [[Creatio ex nihilo|existence out of nothing]]. He thought that all beauty originates from [[God in Christianity|God]] and analyzed it in terms of unity, equality, number, proportion, and order.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Spicher ''Medieval Theories''|loc=§ 3a. St. Augustine}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|p=xxi}} | {{harvnb|Haldane|2013|pp=28–29}} }}</ref> [[Thomas Aquinas]] defined beauty as what brings pleasure upon perception. For him, the mind plays a central role in this process since beauty lies in the immaterial form of the perceived object that the mind recognizes in the sensory data. Aquinas saw beauty as a [[Transcendentals|basic category of being]] and identified it with proportion, radiance, and integrity.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Spicher ''Medieval Theories''|loc=§ 3c. St. Thomas Aquinas}} | {{harvnb|Haldane|2013|pp=33–34}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|p=26}} | {{harvnb|Beardsley|2006|p=47}} }}</ref>

[[File:Alpharabius in Liber Chronicarum 1493 AD.png|thumb|left|upright=0.7|alt=Black-and-white image of an elderly man with a long beard wearing a robe|Artistic woodcut illustration of [[Al-Farabi]], who envisioned beauty as a divine attribute of Allah<ref name="auto11">{{harvnb|Black|1998|loc=Lead section, § 1. Beauty, § 3. Imitation and Imagination}}</ref>]]

An integration of Greek philosophy and religious thought also happened in the [[Islamic world]]. [[Al-Farabi]] ({{circa|878|950 CE}}) associated beauty with pleasure and understood it as a degree of perfection and a divine attribute of [[Allah]]. [[Avicenna]] ({{circa|980}} – 1037 CE) distinguished sensible from intelligible beauty and explored psychological processes underlying aesthetic judgments, such as the role of imagination.<ref name="auto11"/>

Meanwhile, in India, the rasa theory of art expanded to also encompass [[Bhakti|devotional practices]], including efforts to portray or evoke profound religious experiences of the union with the divine.<ref>{{harvnb|Gitomer|1998|p=484}}</ref> For example, [[Abhinavagupta]] ({{circa|950|1025 CE}}) elaborated the spiritual dimension of the rasa theory, drawing a sharp distinction between [[Bhāva (Hinduism)|ordinary worldly emotions]] and rasas as transcendent aesthetic emotions.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Gitomer|1998|pp=484–486}} | {{harvnb|Mee|2018}} }}</ref>

In Chinese thought, [[Xie He (artist)|Xie He]] ({{circa|5th to 6th centuries CE}}) combined [[Daoism|Daoist]] and Confucian ideas, suggesting that artists align with [[Dao|the natural order of the universe]] and spontaneously express the movement of life in their artworks. He also proposed a set of basic principles of painting.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Deutsch|1998|p=410}} | {{harvnb|Higgins|2005|p=685}} }}</ref> [[Guo Xi]] ({{circa|1020|1090 CE}}) argued that artworks reflect the moral character and spiritual outlook of the artist, which he saw as a central factor of the artwork's aesthetic value.<ref>{{harvnb|Deutsch|1998|p=410}}</ref> During this period, the growing influence of [[Buddhism]] on Chinese aesthetic thought led to an artistic shift from objective reality to subjective experiences as a result of Buddhist teachings on the illusory nature of reality.<ref>{{harvnb|Saussy|1998|p=365}}</ref>

The medieval period in the West came to an end with the emergence of the [[Renaissance]] starting in the 15th century. This change led to the revival of classical aesthetic ideals while [[secularization]] paved the way for [[Rationalism|rationalist]] inquiries into general laws of beauty and [[Empiricism|empiricist]] analyses of sensory and emotional experiences in the subsequent [[Age of Enlightenment]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Beardsley|2006|pp=48–49}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=xi–xii, xxiii}} | {{harvnb|Novitz|2013|pp=170–171}} }}</ref>

=== Modern and contemporary ===
[[File:Allan Ramsay - David Hume, 1711 - 1776. Historian and philosopher - Google Art Project.jpg|thumb|upright=0.7|alt=Oil painting showing David Hume from the front against a dark background, dressed in a red coat with gold embroidery, his left arm resting on a surface|[[David Hume]] understood beauty as a pleasurable sentiment and explored taste as the inner sense responsible for this sentiment.<ref name="auto8">{{multiref | {{harvnb|Shelley|2013|pp=40–41}} | {{harvnb|Beardsley|2006|p=51}} | {{harvnb|Janaway|2005d|pp=9–10}} }}</ref>]]

Modern aesthetics emerged in the 18th century, as philosophers engaged more systematically with the subject.<ref>{{harvnb|Shelley|2013|p=36}}</ref> A key step in this process happened through the philosophy of [[Alexander Baumgarten]] (1714–1762), who first conceived aesthetics as a distinct field of inquiry: the science of sensory cognitions or the study of what is sensed and imagined.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Beardsley|2006|pp=49–50}} | {{harvnb|Guyer|2020|loc=Lead section, § 3. Baumgarten and Meier: Aesthetics as the Analogue of Rational Cognition}} }}</ref> In British philosophy, [[Francis Hutcheson (philosopher)|Francis Hutcheson]] (1694–1746) followed ideas of [[Anthony Ashley-Cooper, 3rd Earl of Shaftesbury|the third Earl of Shaftesbury]] (1671–1713) and provided an early theory of taste, conceptualizing it as an internal sense{{efn|Hutcheson distinguished [[Sense|external senses]], which provide ideas about the world, such as vision, from internal senses, which respond to other ideas.<ref>{{harvnb|Dorsey|2021|loc=§ 1.1 The Senses}}</ref>}} responsible for aesthetic apprehension.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Beardsley|2006|p=51}} | {{harvnb|Shelley|2013|pp=37–38}} | {{harvnb|Janaway|2005d|p=9}} }}</ref> This outlook inspired [[David Hume]] (1711–1776) to develop a subjective theory of beauty, understanding it as a pleasurable sentiment caused by perceptions. He combined this perspective with the idea that beauty follows intersubjective standards as shared principles of taste governing which objects are experienced as beautiful.<ref name="auto8"/>

[[Immanuel Kant]] (1724–1804) expanded Hume's idea that aesthetic judgments are both subjective and universal, arguing that the underlying pleasure must be disinterested to follow universal standards. According to Kant, this type of pleasure comes from a free play in which the mental faculties of imagination and understanding harmoniously interact.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Shelley|2013|pp=46–47}} | {{harvnb|Janaway|2005d|p=10}} }}</ref> In response to earlier theories by [[Edmund Burke]] (1729–1797), Kant also examined the sublime as a distinct aesthetic quality.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Shelley|2013|p=51}} | {{harvnb|Doran|2015|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=B9koCgAAQBAJ&pg=PA240 240]}} }}</ref>

Kant's thought inspired diverse developments in [[German philosophy]]. [[Friedrich Schiller]] (1759–1805) saw art as a unifying phenomenon that synthesizes different basic human drives in a type of play.<ref name="auto1">{{multiref | {{harvnb|Janaway|2005d|p=10}} | {{harvnb|Beardsley|2006|p=54}} }}</ref> [[F. W. J. von Schelling]] (1775–1854) shared a similar perspective, arguing that art reconciles opposites and reveals the underlying unity of the self and nature.<ref name="auto1"/> [[G. W. F. Hegel]] (1770–1831) studied aesthetics through his philosophical system of [[absolute idealism]], seeing artistic beauty as the sensory manifestation of truth.<ref name="auto16">{{multiref | {{harvnb|Janaway|2005d|pp=10–11}} | {{harvnb|Beardsley|2006|p=54}} }}</ref>{{efn|Hegel also analyzed [[art history]] from antiquity to his present day as a series of progressive stages of this manifestation.<ref name="auto16"/>}}

Combining [[Kantianism|Kantian]] and Indian philosophy, [[Arthur Schopenhauer]] (1788–1860) understood disinterested aesthetic experience as a suspension of the will, resulting in a temporary peace of mind by interrupting the cycle of striving and suffering.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Janaway|2005d|p=11}} | {{harvnb|Beardsley|2006|pp=55–56}} }}</ref> He inspired the Chinese philosopher [[Wang Guowei]] (1877–1927), who integrated Schopenhauer's ideas with Buddhist thought. Wang viewed the goal of art as the creation of worlds within the world, which are open to disinterested reflection.<ref>{{harvnb|Saussy|1998|p=3367}}</ref> [[Friedrich Nietzsche]] (1844–1900) rejected the disinterestedness of aesthetic experience and the autonomy of art from other domains. Instead, he considered art an expression of the struggle between [[Apollonian and Dionysian|opposing life forces]], seeing it as a vehicle of transformation and [[life affirmation]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=224–226}} | {{harvnb|Janaway|2005d|p=11}} | {{harvnb|Gama|2008|pp=67–73}} }}</ref>

Following the thought of [[Karl Marx]] (1818–1883), [[Marxist aesthetics|Marxist aesthetic philosophers]] like [[Leon Trotsky]] (1879–1940) and [[Georg Lukács]] (1885–1971) examined how art reflects and shapes social ideologies and power hierarchies.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Guyer|2006|pp=68–69}} | {{harvnb|Munro|Scruton|2025|loc=§ Marxist Aesthetics}} }}</ref> Drawing from Marxist ideas, [[Theodor Adorno]] (1903–1969) critiqued the [[commodification]] of art and explored its ability to express [[Social alienation|alienation]] and challenge societal norms.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Guyer|2006|pp=69–70}} | {{harvnb|Janaway|2005d|p=12}} | {{harvnb|Benčin|2023|pp=[http://www.scielo.org.co/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S0121-36282023000200031 31–33]}} }}</ref> Also adopting a Marxist perspective, [[Walter Benjamin]] (1892–1940) studied how advances in technological reproducibility transform art.<ref>{{harvnb|Osborne|Charles|2021|loc=§ 6. Art and Technology}}</ref>{{efn|He explored, for example, to what extent mass production errodes [[authenticity in art]] and how [[Aestheticization of politics|it is used for political purposes]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Osborne|Charles|2021|loc=§ 6. Art and Technology}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=48–49}} | {{harvnb|Hall|2006|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=sk3o1irXY5oC&pg=PA90 90]}} }}</ref>}}

[[File:Heidegger 3 (1960).jpg|thumb|upright|alt=Black-and-white photo of a man wearing a suit and a tie|[[Martin Heidegger]] proposed that art can uncover fundamental aspects of human existence.<ref name="Thomson 2024">{{multiref | {{harvnb|Thomson|2024|loc=Lead section, § 2. Heidegger's Philosophical Critique of Aesthetics: Introduction, § 3.7 Heidegger's Post-Modern Understanding of Art}} | {{harvnb|Wartenberg|2013|pp=116–120}} }}</ref>]]

[[Romanticism|Romanticist]] thought emphasized artistic originality, creativity, and the expression of profound feelings, as formulated in the works of [[J. W. von Goethe]] (1749–1832), [[William Wordsworth]] (1770–1850), and [[Samuel Taylor Coleridge]] (1772–1834). It saw artworks as products of human [[genius]] that defy rule-based understanding.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=272–273}} | {{harvnb|Beardsley|2006|pp=54–55}} }}</ref> This school of thought inspired the theory of expressionism, which asserts that the primary function of art is to communicate emotions and other mental states. It was examined by thinkers such as [[Leo Tolstoy]] (1828–1910), [[Benedetto Croce]] (1866–1952), and [[R. G. Collingwood]] (1889–1943).<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|p=114}} | {{harvnb|Shimamura|2012|p=9}} | {{harvnb|Lyas|1998|pp=474–476}} }}</ref> Intentionalism, a closely related position, focuses on the author's intent as the source of meaning of artworks.
