[[Monroe Beardsley]] (1915–1985) opposed this view, arguing that meaning is not fixed by private intentions.<ref>{{harvnb|Townsend|2006|p=45}}</ref> [[Sigmund Freud]] (1856–1939) and [[Carl Jung]] (1875–1961) interpreted art through a [[Psychoanalysis|psychoanalytic]] perspective as expressions of [[the unconscious]], an approach also later explored by [[Richard Wollheim]] (1923–2005).<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=258–259}} | {{harvnb|Geller|1993|pp=377–378}} }}</ref>

In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, [[aestheticism]] became a prominent view in English-speaking philosophy. For example, [[Walter Pater]] (1839–1894) and [[Oscar Wilde]] (1854–1900) proposed that [[art for art's sake|art is an end in itself]] without an ulterior purpose.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Janaway|2005d|p=12}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=234, 327}} }}</ref> [[Pragmatism|Pragmatists]] rejected this outlook and the idea that aesthetic experience is disinterested. For instance, [[John Dewey]] (1859–1952) proposed in his 1934 book ''[[Art as Experience]]'' that the value of art lies in the unique experiences it provides, which can lead to individual and societal improvements.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=253–254}} | {{harvnb|Beardsley|2006|pp=57–58}} | {{harvnb|Viale|Campeotto|2021|pp=117–121}} }}</ref> [[Formalism (art)|Formalism]] became another influential theory of art in the early 20th century. It dismisses the focus on expressive and representational aspects and argues instead that artworks are defined by formal features, like the arrangement of perceptual qualities. [[Clive Bell]] (1881–1964), a major proponent of this view, termed this arrangement "[[significant form]]".<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Shimamura|2012|pp=9–10}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=126–127}} }}</ref>

The emergence of [[Dadaism]] and [[conceptual art]] challenged traditional definitions of art based on intrinsic features of artworks.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Adajian|2024|loc=§ 4. Contemporary Definitions}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=73–74, 83}} | {{harvnb|Lamarque|2013b|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=wYoeAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA773 773–774]}}}}</ref> As a result, anti-essentialism, which understands art as a category fixed by social or interpretative conventions without an inherent [[essence]], gained prominence in the second half of the 20th century in [[analytic philosophy]], exemplified in the theories of [[Nelson Goodman]] (1906–1998), [[Morris Weitz]] (1916–1981), and [[Frank Sibley (philosopher)|Frank Sibley]] (1923–1996).<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Janaway|2005d|p=12}} | {{harvnb|Dickie|2012|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=C4wrBgAAQBAJ&pg=PA277 277]}} | {{harvnb|Giovannelli|2017|loc=§ 4. From Languages of Art to Reconceptions: New Looks at Aesthetic Issues}} | {{harvnb|Davies|2018|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=9pNlDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA4 4–6]}} }}</ref> These developments inspired [[Arthur C. Danto]] (1924–2013) and [[George Dickie (philosopher)|George Dickie]] (1926–2020) to propose institutional definitions, arguing that social conventions set by the [[art world]] determine which objects are artworks.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Adajian|2024|loc=§ 4.2 Institutional Definitions}} | {{harvnb|Guyer|2006|pp=66–67}} | {{harvnb|Janaway|2005d|p=13}} }}</ref> [[Mary Mothersill]] (1923–2008) challenged these developments. She aimed to restore earlier conceptions of beauty associated with Aquinas, Hume, and Kant, focusing on the apprehension of aesthetic qualities.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Guyer|2006|p=67}} | {{harvnb|Guyer|1986|pp=245–246}} }}</ref>

In [[continental philosophy]], the school of [[Phenomenology (philosophy)|phenomenology]] studied the immediate experience of art. For example, it examined how artworks can depict unreal objects, how imagination is involved in the process, and how art can reveal features of reality.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Chaplin|2013|pp=126–128, 133–134}} | {{harvnb|Beardsley|2006|p=59}} }}</ref> This tradition is closely related to [[Existentialism|existentialist]] aesthetics, which views artworks as expressions of human freedom that can authentically portray central aspects of the [[human condition]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Deranty|2025|loc=Lead section}} | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|pp=111–112}} }}</ref> The philosophy of [[Martin Heidegger]] (1889–1976) influenced both traditions. He criticized the focus on disinterested pleasure found in modern philosophy of art, arguing that artworks can reveal truths about human existence and provide new perspectives of understanding.<ref name="Thomson 2024"/> Heidegger's student [[Hans-Georg Gadamer]] (1900–2002) further investigated the relation between art and truth, examining aesthetic experience and traditional theories through phenomenological analysis and [[Hermeneutics|hermeneutic]] interpretation.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Townsend|2006|p=131}} | {{harvnb|Davey|Nielsen|2023|loc=Lead section}} }}</ref>

[[Postmodern philosophy|Postmodern thinkers]], like [[Roland Barthes]] (1915–1980) and [[Jacques Derrida]] (1930–2004), challenged the separation of art from everyday life and the idea that artworks have a stable meaning or universal value. They suggested instead that artistic merit depends on historical and cultural contexts.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Novitz|2013|pp=171–173, 177}} | {{harvnb|Shusterman|2005|pp=771–772, 781–782}} }}</ref> Starting in the 1970s, [[Feminist aesthetics|feminist perspectives]] challenged male-centric theories and practices within aesthetic philosophy and the art world. For example, [[Simone de Beauvoir]] (1908–1986) and [[Luce Irigaray]] (born 1930) explored how feminine perspectives are marginalized by masculine standards.<ref>{{harvnb|Korsmeyer|Weiser|2021|loc=Lead section, § 1. Art and Artists: Historical Background, § 3. Aesthetic Categories and Feminist Critiques, § 5. The Body in Art and Philosophy}}</ref>
